course_description_html: Welcome back! In this module, we will open the chassis and examine the specific mechanical and solid-state technologies driving these systems. We will compare the real-world performance of robotic actuators, microscopic mirrors, and silicon waveguides to see exactly how these physical connections are made.

blocks.body_html:
The sheer scale of modern artificial intelligence workloads is forcing a physical reckoning within data center fabrics. Traditional electrical packet switching is rapidly approaching its thermal and latency limits.

Optical Circuit Switching encompasses a variety of distinct hardware technologies. In this module, we will explore the physical mechanisms driving these systems and evaluate their architectural tradeoffs.

blocks.heading_html: By the end of this module, you will be able to:

items_html: Identify the six primary OCS switching technologies.
Describe the fundamental operating principles of each technology family.
Compare key performance characteristics including switching speed, port count, insertion loss, and power profile.

blocks.body_html:
Optical Circuit Switching relies on several distinct underlying technologies to physically route light.

Let's begin by defining the primary technology families currently shaping the OCS landscape.

Explore the tabs below to learn more about the different components that make up the OCS technology families.

items.title: Robotic Mechanisms
items.description_html: These systems function like automated fiber patch panels. Motorized components physically move and connect fiber cables. They support very large port counts and provide a passive holding state without requiring power, but their reconfiguration times range from seconds to minutes.

items.title: MEMS Mirrors
items.description_html: Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems use tiny, tiltable mirrors to steer light beams in free space. They offer millisecond switching times and support large port counts. They are widely deployed at scale, notably within Google's TPUv4 supercomputer clusters.

items.title: Liquid Crystal
items.description_html: These solid-state devices electronically control light paths by manipulating optical polarization. They require no moving parts and operate in the milliseconds switching speed

items.title: Piezoelectric
items.description_html: These mechanisms use voltage to deform specialized materials, creating highly precise physical motions to align fibers or mirrors. They are capable of microsecond switching speeds.

items.title: Silicon Photonics (Waveguide-based)
items.description_html:
This technology routes light through submicron on-chip waveguides using thermo-optic or electro-optic effects.

It offers extremely fast nanosecond to microsecond switching times and chip-scale integration, but it faces higher insertion loss and scaling challenges, although integrating Semiconductor Optical Amplifier (SOA) can help compensate for these losses.

items.title: Metasurface
items.description_html: This approach steers collimated beams in free space without mechanical motion. It uses electrically tunable sub-wavelength pixels to control optical phase, with the potential for high port density and fast switching, depending on the device design and technology maturity.

items.title: Hybrid/Combinations
items.description_html: These systems integrate multiple mechanisms, such as combining Silicon Photonics with MEMS micro-actuators, to optimize the trade-offs between actuation speed and insertion loss.

blocks.heading_html: Knowing the underlying mechanism is important, but network architects must evaluate these technologies against strict performance metrics.

Because each hardware approach offers distinct strengths regarding port density and actuation speed, they naturally align with different tiers of the data center.

Explore the interactive cards below to connect each technology with its optimal architectural use case.

back.description_html: Moves physical fiber cables. Best for massive scale patching with a zero-power hold state.
Physically tilts microscopic mirrors. Best for large radix, millisecond-scale dynamic topologies.
Manipulates optical polarization without moving parts. Best for compact, low-power solid-state switching.
Deforms materials using voltage for precise alignment. Best for fast microsecond precision steering.

Routes light through on-chip waveguides. Best for ultra-fast microsecond to nanosecond switching, though insertion loss is a key trade-off, integrating Semiconductor Optical Amplifiers (SOAs) can help compensate these losses.
Steers light using tunable sub-wavelength pixels. Best for fast, high-density free-space routing without mechanical motion.

blocks.body_html:
Knowing the underlying mechanism is important, but network architects must evaluate these technologies against strict performance metrics.

Explore the matrix below to compare how the different OCS technologies perform across critical networking dimensions.

items.caption_html:
Switching Speed

Silicon Photonics leads with nanosecond to microsecond speeds. Liquid Crystal and Piezoelectric systems also operate rapidly in the milliseconds range.

MEMS systems typically operate in the millisecond range. Robotic mechanisms are the slowest, taking seconds to minutes.

Port Count (Radix)

Robotic mechanisms support very large port counts.

MEMS technologies reliably support large port counts. Silicon Photonics typically supports low to medium port counts due to insertion loss scaling.

Insertion Loss

Robotic, Liquid Crystal, and Piezoelectric systems offer low insertion loss.

MEMS offers low to medium loss. Silicon Photonics suffers from higher insertion loss, which often requires integrated semiconductor optical amplifiers.

Moving Parts

Robotic and MEMS technologies rely on physical mechanical motion.

Liquid Crystal, Silicon Photonics, and Metasurface technologies are solid-state and require no moving parts.

lessons.title: Knowledge Check
lessons.description_html:
Let's test your understanding on the OCS technologies and use cases.

Select "Start Quiz" to begin.

blocks.question_html: Which OCS technology consumes zero power to maintain its switching state once it is set?
blocks.feedback_correct_html: Correct. Robotic mechanisms feature mechanical, latching connections that remain intact without power once established.
blocks.feedback_incorrect_html: Incorrect. Robotic mechanisms use latching connections that hold their physical state without requiring electrical power.

blocks.question_html: A network architect needs sub-millisecond reconfiguration for a dynamic AI cluster. Which two technology families are most appropriate?

choices.text_html: 3D MEMS and Robotic Fiber Patch Panels
Liquid Crystal on Silicon (LCoS) and Piezoelectric Actuators.

blocks.feedback_correct_html: Correct. Both Silicon Photonics and Metasurfaces eliminate moving mechanical parts entirely. By relying on solid-state manipulation of light, they enable the nanosecond reconfiguration speeds necessary for highly dynamic workloads.
blocks.feedback_incorrect_html: Incorrect. Mechanical solutions like 3D MEMS or robotic actuators physically move components, limiting them to slower millisecond switching times. Silicon Photonics and Metasurfaces are the correct choices because they provide solid-state, nanosecond switching.

blocks.question_html: True or False: Silicon Photonics OCS requires physical moving parts to redirect optical signals.
blocks.feedback_correct_html: Correct. Silicon Photonics is a solid-state technology that uses thermo-optic or electro-optic effects to route light without moving parts.
blocks.feedback_incorrect_html: Incorrect. Silicon Photonics uses entirely solid-state phase shifting without any physical moving components.

blocks.question_html: What is the key functional tradeoff that worsens as port counts (radix) increase across most OCS technology types?
blocks.feedback_correct_html: Correct. As radix increases, optical insertion loss typically increases, limiting the practical scale of the switch without optical amplification.
blocks.feedback_incorrect_html: Incorrect. Insertion loss is the primary constraint that worsens as you scale up the port count on an optical switch.

blocks.body_html:
Great job! You have completed this module. With a firm grasp on the underlying hardware, we are ready to explore how these switches operate in the real world.

Here are some key takeaways on OCS technology families and components:

items_html: OCS technologies include Robotic, MEMS, Liquid Crystal, Piezoelectric, Silicon Photonics, Metasurface, and Hybrid systems.
MEMS is the mature, widely deployed standard for large port counts, utilizing physical mirrors.
Silicon Photonics offers nanosecond switching speeds without moving parts but faces higher insertion loss scaling.
